details:
**Ninety-Five Theses (1517)**
Luther's list of propositions attacking the sale of indulgences. According to tradition, he nailed it to the door of the Castle Church in Wittenberg, and it is usually treated as the start of the Protestant Reformation. One thesis asks why the pope, whose wealth exceeds that of the richest Crassus, does not build St. Peter's Basilica with his own money instead of the money of poor believers.

**Diet of Worms and "Here I stand, I can do no other"**
The 1521 imperial assembly before Emperor Charles V where Luther was ordered to recant his writings. He sorted his books into categories (works of faith that even his enemies accepted, attacks on the papacy and its abuses, and attacks on individual opponents) and refused to retract any of them. He reportedly ended with "Here I stand, I can do no other," although that line may be apocryphal. The resulting Edict of Worms declared him an outlaw.

**Johann Tetzel and indulgences**
Tetzel was the Dominican friar whose aggressive preaching of indulgences near Wittenberg provoked Luther; he is linked to the jingle "As soon as the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs." The campaign raised money for rebuilding St. Peter's Basilica and to pay off the debts of Archbishop Albert (Albrecht) of Mainz.

**Exsurge Domine and Pope Leo X**
The 1520 papal bull issued by Leo X that condemned 41 of Luther's propositions and gave him 60 days to recant. It opens by asking God to "arise" and "judge your own cause" against a "wild boar from the forest" ravaging the Lord's vineyard. Luther publicly burned it, and he was formally excommunicated by the follow-up bull Decet Romanum Pontificem in 1521.

**Marburg Colloquy (1529)**
A meeting arranged by Philip of Hesse to unite the German and Swiss Protestants, where Luther debated Ulrich Zwingli over the Eucharist. Luther insisted that Christ's body and blood are really present in the bread and wine, while Zwingli held that they are symbolic, and the two sides failed to agree.

**German Peasants' War and Against the Murderous, Thieving Hordes of Peasants**
The 1524–1525 uprising, partly inspired by Luther's ideas and associated with the radical preacher Thomas Müntzer. Luther turned against the rebels and urged the princes to crush them, calling them "filthy swine" and "mad dogs" in his pamphlet Against the Murderous, Thieving Hordes of Peasants.

**On the Jews and Their Lies**
Luther's 1543 antisemitic treatise urging authorities to burn synagogues, destroy Jewish homes and forbid rabbis to teach. It contrasts sharply with his earlier, friendlier 1523 work That Jesus Christ Was Born a Jew, which called the Jews blood relatives of Christ.

**Wartburg Castle and the German Bible**
After the Diet of Worms, Luther was "kidnapped" for his own protection and hidden for about a year in Wartburg Castle near Eisenach. There he translated the New Testament into German (published 1522), the start of his full German Bible.

**Frederick the Wise**
Frederick III, Elector of Saxony, was Luther's protector. He secured Luther safe conduct to the Diet of Worms and arranged his hiding at the Wartburg.

**Katharina von Bora**
A former Cistercian nun who escaped her convent and married Luther in 1525. She managed their household and finances in Wittenberg, and she called her husband "Sir Doctor" ("Herr Doktor").

**"A Mighty Fortress Is Our God"**
Luther's most famous hymn ("Ein feste Burg ist unser Gott"), based on Psalm 46. Its lyrics include "The Spirit and the gifts are ours through Him who with us sideth."

**Vow to St. Anne in a thunderstorm**
In 1505, while studying law, Luther was caught in a violent thunderstorm and cried out "Help, St. Anne! I will become a monk!" He then left law school and entered the Augustinian monastery at Erfurt.

**Cardinal Cajetan**
Thomas Cajetan was the papal legate who questioned Luther at Augsburg in 1518 and demanded that he recant. Luther refused and slipped out of the city.

**Philip Melanchthon and the Loci Communes**
Melanchthon was Luther's closest colleague at Wittenberg. His Loci Communes (1521) was the first systematic presentation of Lutheran theology, built around justification by faith alone, and he later wrote the Augsburg Confession.

**Small and Large Catechisms and the Schmalkald Articles**
Luther wrote his Small and Large Catechisms in 1529 to teach the basics of the faith to ordinary people and to pastors. He drafted the Schmalkald Articles in 1537 as a summary of Lutheran doctrine for the Schmalkaldic League of Protestant princes.
